title: Why Do Golf Balls Have Dimples?

fin.small: Sources: J. Choi, W.-P. Jeon, H. Choi, Physics of Fluids 18, 041702, 2006; N. Beratlis, E. Balaras and K. Squires, Journal of Fluid Mechanics 879, 2019; W. Taylor, US Patent 878,254, 1908; Wikipedia, 'Golf ball'.

parts: Little dents can cut a test ball's air drag in half. How can rough beat smooth?
Stay for the odd thing dents do to air.
In the eighteen hundreds, a new golf ball was molded from rubbery tree sap.
The usual story: scuffed old balls flew more steadily than smooth new ones.
So, the story goes, makers began marking new balls on purpose.
In 1906, English engineer William Taylor filed a US patent for shallow round hollows, evenly spread.
Here is why. Dimples stir up the thin layer of air hugging the ball.
Stirred air clings longer, so the wake behind shrinks, and so does drag.
It's well established: on a sphere, dimples can cut drag by more than half, at certain speeds.
So at those speeds, rough wins: the air holds on longer. Subscribe for the next one.
